screens.title: Reentrancy and Integer Over/Underflows
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn two classes of vulnerabilities that have repeatedly caused large losses in smart contracts: reentrancy and integer over/underflows. We'll build a mental model for how external calls can be abused to re-enter a function before state updates happen, and how low-level integer arithmetic can silently wrap values in older Solidity versions. You will see concrete vulnerable examples, step through an exploit pattern, and learn practical mitigations you can apply immediately: the Checks-Effects-Interactions ordering, using reentrancy guards, and relying on Solidity 0.8.0's built-in arithmetic checks or SafeMath for legacy code. Knowing these patterns matters because defenses are simple to apply but, when omitted, they enable trivial automatic drains and token minting bugs. As you follow the examples, think of each rule as a small discipline: update state before sending funds, lock critical functions while executing, and prefer compiler-level checks for arithmetic. By the end you'll be able to identify risky code, fix it, and design tests that simulate real attacker behavior.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: This first set of objectives focuses on reentrancy and immediate defenses. First, you'll be able to identify a reentrancy vulnerability by recognizing external calls that happen before state updates and the classic withdrawal pattern that allows callbacks. You'll also learn to implement the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern so that state is adjusted before any external calls happen, preventing reentry-based drains. Third, you'll adopt a reentrancy guard pattern or mutex to lock functions during execution, which is a complementary protection in more complex flows. Finally, you'll practice analyzing real-world exploit scenarios to see how simple ordering mistakes become catastrophic when combined with attacker contracts. Each objective emphasizes not only what to change in code but why that change prevents the exploit. For example, updating balances before sending Ether removes the attacker's ability to withdraw repeatedly because the invariant that the contract relies on has already been modified. These skills are practical: you'll use them when reviewing withdrawals, escrow flows, or any function that interacts with external addresses.

screens.title: What is Reentrancy?
screens.narratorSegment: Reentrancy is a class of vulnerability that happens when a contract makes an external call and the callee is able to call back into the original contract before the original function has finished updating its internal state. The key problem is timing: the contract assumes that once it calls out, the rest of the function runs in isolation, but an attacker can break that assumption by implementing a fallback or receive function that calls back. A helpful analogy is a vending machine that dispenses a soda before updating its inventory. If you can repeatedly trigger the dispenser before the inventory count is decremented, you can get more sodas than you paid for. In Solidity, calls such as low-level call with value or transfer can invoke code on the recipient. If the recipient is a malicious contract with a callback that re-enters the withdraw function, it can withdraw multiple times while the balance still indicates available funds. Concrete example: a withdrawal function that sends Ether and then decrements the user's balance is vulnerable because the decrement hasn't happened when the external call executes. A common misconception is that the Ethereum transaction model serializes everything and prevents reentry; it does not. Transactions are atomic at the EVM level, but external calls execute user-defined code which can call back into any public or external function on the original contract during the same transaction. The core takeaway is to never rely on state that will be changed after an external call. Instead, order your operations so the contract's internal invariants are preserved before making external calls.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Reentrancy occurs when external calls allow the callee to call back into the caller before it finalizes state updates, enabling repeated effects.

content.html:
Core Concept › What is Reentrancy?

A concise definition and metaphor

Reentrancy lets a callee call back into the caller before it finalizes state changes. The vending machine analogy shows the risk: dispensing before deducting.

Key points
  • External calls can execute attacker code that calls back into your contract.
  • If you update state after an external call, the attacker can re-enter and exploit the unchanged state.
  • Atomic transactions don't prevent reentry because callbacks run in the same transaction before state update.
Analogy
Think of dispensing goods before charging the customer. Quick re-entry lets the attacker take more goods than paid for.
Concrete check
When reviewing withdrawals, ensure the balance is updated before sending value. If you see an external call followed by a decrement, flag it as vulnerable.
Common misconception
Believing transfer or gas limits always protect you is risky. Some external calls still allow reentry through fallback functions in many contexts.
Key Takeaway

Treat any external call as potentially malicious and order state updates before it.

screens.title: Vulnerable Withdrawal Example
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a short vulnerable withdrawal contract so you can see exactly what to look for in code. The core pattern is: check balance, send Ether via a call, then update the balance. The problem is that the external call gives control to the recipient before the balance is decremented. In our vulnerable example the function uses a low-level call to send Ether and only after confirming success does it subtract from the sender's balance. An attacker implements a fallback that calls withdraw again. Because the balance has not changed, the second call passes the require and sends Ether again. This repeats until the contract's Ether is drained or gas runs out. When you read real code, watch for any use of msg. sender. call{value:...} or transfer followed by state changes. Even if transfer imposes a gas stipend, complex interactions or proxy patterns can still present windows for reentry. The correct fix will reorder the operations and optionally add a reentrancy guard. As you study this snippet, imagine an attacker contract that calls withdraw from its fallback. That mental model helps you write tests that mimic the exploit.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough › VulnerableWithdrawal

Vulnerable withdrawal pattern

Solidity example (vulnerable)
<!-- code -->
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract VulnerableWithdrawal {
    mapping(address => uint) public balances;

    constructor() payable {
        balances[msg.sender] = msg.value;
    }

    function deposit() public payable {
        balances[msg.sender] += msg.value;
    }

    function withdraw(uint _amount) public {
        require(balances[msg.sender] >= _amount, "Insufficient balance");

        // VULNERABLE: External call before state update
        (bool success, ) = msg.sender.call{value: _amount}("");
        require(success, "Withdrawal failed");

        balances[msg.sender] -= _amount; // State updated AFTER external call
    }

    function getBalance() public view returns (uint) {
        return address(this).balance;
    }
}
Explanation
  • The external call occurs before the balance is decreased, which creates the reentry window.
  • A malicious recipient can run code to call withdraw again inside its fallback, while the balance still appears unchanged.
  • Tests should deploy an attacker contract with a fallback that calls withdraw to emulate the exploit.
Example scenario
If an attacker deposited 1 ether and then re-entered withdraw for 1 ether repeatedly, the contract can be drained.
Common mistake

Assuming a transfer or call is safe without reordering state updates is a frequent oversight.

screens.title: Reentrancy Exploit Sequence
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the exploit sequence helps you design tests and mitigations. The attack begins when the attacker deposits funds into the victim contract or otherwise gains a valid balance. Next the attacker calls the vulnerable withdraw function. The function performs the require check and then immediately performs an external call to send Ether. At that moment control passes to the attacker contract, which implements a fallback or receive handler that calls withdraw again. Because the original function has not yet decremented the attacker's balance, the check still passes and another external transfer occurs. The attacker repeats this call sequence until the victim contract's balance is drained. Tests that demonstrate this pattern should include an attacker contract that calls back during the external call and assertions that the victim's balance decreases while the attacker's internal accounting grows incorrectly. A common mitigation step is to reorder steps so state is updated before the external call, breaking the exploit sequence. Locks, such as a reentrancy guard, also interrupt the repeated calls by preventing the second call from entering the same function while it is already running. Thinking in sequences teaches you to close each reentry window.

keyIdea.title: Attack steps
keyIdea.text: Deposit → call withdraw → external call triggers fallback → fallback calls withdraw again → repeat until drained.

content.html:
Process Flow › Exploit Sequence

Exploit sequence: numbered steps

  1. Attacker funds the contract. The attacker gets legitimate balance.
  2. Attacker calls withdraw. The victim contract validates and then makes an external call to the attacker.
  3. Fallback triggers callback. The attacker contract's fallback calls withdraw again before the victim updates balances.
  4. Repeated withdrawals. Steps 2–3 loop until the victim contract is drained or gas is exhausted.
Design tests that deploy both contracts and assert that the vulnerable contract's balance drops to zero while the attacker receives multiple transfers in a single transaction.
Mitigations
  • Apply Checks-Effects-Interactions: update balances before external calls.
  • Use a reentrancy guard to prevent nested calls during execution.
  • Minimize logic during external calls; prefer pull over push patterns when possible.
Pro tip

When writing tests, assert that a reentrancy attack transaction reverts or fails against your fixed contract.

screens.title: Checks-Effects-Interactions in Practice
screens.narratorSegment: The Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern is the simplest and most widely recommended defense against reentrancy. It prescribes ordering: first perform all checks, then make state changes, and only finally interact with external contracts. This ensures that if an external call attempts to reenter, the necessary state invariants have already been updated and the reentry fails or has no effect. In practice this means moving balance decrements ahead of Ether transfers or external calls. Another common refinement is to use a withdraw-pull pattern: let users request a balance and then pull funds themselves rather than the contract pushing funds automatically. The corrected SecureWithdrawal example demonstrates this: the require check is done, the balance is decremented, and then the external call is executed. Also consider adding a reentrancy guard as an additional safety net. When you refactor code, run the same exploit tests against the new contract. A correctly refactored contract will not allow the attacker fallback to withdraw again because the balance no longer permits it. Remember that ordering and invariants are your first line of defense. Checks-Effects-Interactions in Practice means checks first, update state second, call external addresses last to close reentrancy windows.. In practical terms, refactor the vulnerable function to prevent reentrancy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Secure Pattern › Checks-Effects-Interactions

Refactored withdrawal

Solidity example (secure)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract SecureWithdrawal {
    mapping(address => uint) public balances;

    constructor() payable {
        balances[msg.sender] = msg.value;
    }

    function deposit() public payable {
        balances[msg.sender] += msg.value;
    }

    function withdraw(uint _amount) public {
        // 1. Checks
        require(balances[msg.sender] >= _amount, "Insufficient balance");

        // 2. Effects
        balances[msg.sender] -= _amount;

        // 3. Interactions
        (bool success, ) = msg.sender.call{value: _amount}("");
        require(success, "Withdrawal failed");
    }

    function getBalance() public view returns (uint) {
        return address(this).balance;
    }
}
Refactor notes
  • Move state updates before external calls to ensure invariants hold during callbacks.
  • Prefer the pull pattern where feasible: let users call withdraw themselves.
  • Run exploit tests to verify the attack no longer succeeds.
Key Takeaway

Ordering changes are simple and effective: update state first, then call out.

screens.title: Reentrancy Guards and Mutexes
screens.narratorSegment: A reentrancy guard is a simple pattern that uses a state variable as a mutex to prevent a function from being entered while it is already executing. OpenZeppelin's ReentrancyGuard is a common implementation: it sets a status flag when entering a protected function and clears it on exit. If a reentrant call tries to enter while the flag is set, the guard reverts. This approach is particularly useful when complex state updates or multiple external calls make a pure ordering solution difficult. However, guards should be used thoughtfully: they add a global lock for the function, which can change contract behavior in legitimate nested scenarios. In practice, combine a guard with Checks-Effects-Interactions for robust protection. A common misconception is that a guard alone is always sufficient; it is a strong safety net, but correct ordering and minimal external calls are still best practices. When writing tests, protect a function with a guard and confirm that an attacker fallback causes a revert instead of permitting repeated withdrawals. The guard provides clarity: if any nested call attempts to re-enter, the contract explicitly denies it.

keyIdea.title: Guard idea
keyIdea.text: A mutex-style status variable blocks reentry by reverting if a protected function is already running.

content.html:
Definition › Reentrancy Guard

Lock functions to prevent nested execution

How it works
  • Set a status variable when entering the function.
  • If the function is called again while the status is set, revert immediately.
  • Clear the status variable on successful exit.
Guards are simple and auditable, and they complement ordering rules to give layered defense.
When to use
  • When functions perform multiple interactions and ordering alone is hard to guarantee.
  • To add a safety net during refactors or when exposing many external hooks.
  • Not as a substitute for clear state invariants—use both approaches together.
Misconception check

A guard prevents reentry but does not make insecure logic safe; you still must check and update state correctly.

screens.title: External Calls: call vs transfer
screens.narratorSegment: When sending Ether from a contract you will commonly see three mechanisms: transfer, send, and call with value. Historically transfer forwarded a fixed, small gas stipend and was considered safer against reentrancy because it limited what the recipient could do in its fallback. However, that gas stipend is often insufficient for modern recipient contracts and can cause failures. The low-level call with value is now the most common pattern because it forwards all available gas, which is necessary for interacting with complex recipient logic, but it also creates a larger reentrancy surface because the callee has more gas to run arbitrary code including callbacks. The key point is that the choice of call mechanism is orthogonal to the ordering rule: even a transfer can be problematic if the contract relies on state updates happening later. Thus you should write code assuming any external call may execute complicated logic. Prefer call with value when you need it, but always update critical state and, where appropriate, combine this with a reentrancy guard. Tests should exercise calls with realistic gas assumptions to ensure an attacker can or cannot perform reentry as expected. Don't rely on gas limits as your primary defense.

keyIdea.title: Practical choice
keyIdea.text: Use call with value when needed, but never assume gas behavior prevents reentrancy. Order and guards are primary defenses.

content.html:
Comparison › call vs transfer

External call mechanisms and risk

transfer
Forwards small fixed gas; can break with complex recipients but historically limited reentrancy capability.
send
Similar to transfer but returns a boolean instead of reverting; requires explicit checks.
call{value:...}()
Forwards all remaining gas; flexible but requires careful ordering and guards to prevent reentry.
Key rule: choose the mechanism for compatibility, but never treat gas limits as a security pattern. Always order state updates and consider a reentrancy guard.

screens.title: Integer Overflow and Underflow
screens.narratorSegment: Integer overflow happens when an arithmetic operation produces a value larger than the type can represent and the value wraps around to the minimum. Integer underflow is the opposite: an operation results in a value below the minimum and wraps to the maximum. In unsigned integers used throughout Solidity, underflow often wraps to a very large number. For example, on an 8-bit unsigned integer, incrementing 255 yields 0; decrementing 0 yields 255. In token accounting this wrap-around can lead to effectively minting large balances or zeroing out supply checks. Before Solidity 0.8.0 these operations did not revert automatically, and developers relied on libraries like SafeMath to explicitly check for dangerous conditions before performing arithmetic. A common misconception is assuming that require checks like balances[msg. sender] - amount >= 0 will protect you; in older solc versions subtraction underflow happens prior to the comparison, which invalidates the guard. The practical advice is to use Solidity 0.8.0 or later to get built-in checks, and in legacy code adopt SafeMath or equivalent checks. Always include tests that attempt out-of-range arithmetic to ensure your contract reverts instead of silently wrapping.

In token accounting this wrap-around can lead to effectively minting large balances or zeroing out supply checks. Before Solidity 0.8.0 these operations did not revert automatically, and developers relied on libraries like SafeMath to explicitly check for dangerous conditions before performing arithmetic. A common misconception is assuming that require checks like balances[msg. sender] - amount >= 0 will protect you; in older solc versions subtraction underflow happens prior to the comparison, which invalidates the guard. The practical advice is to use Solidity 0.8.0 or later to get built-in checks, and in legacy code adopt SafeMath or equivalent checks. Always include tests that attempt out-of-range arithmetic to ensure your contract reverts instead of silently wrapping.

keyIdea.title: Wrap-around

content.html:
Core Concept › Integer Overflow & Underflow

Wrap-around arithmetic explained

Illustration (uint8)
If x is uint8 and x == 255, then x + 1 wraps to 0. If x == 0 and you compute x - 1, it wraps to 255. In token math this can create huge unintended balances.
Misconception check

A subtraction check written as balances[msg.sender] - amount >= 0 is unsafe in older compilers because the underflow happens before the comparison.

Practical advice
  • Prefer Solidity 0.8.0+ for automatic reverts on overflow/underflow.
  • In legacy code, wrap arithmetic in SafeMath-style checks that revert on bad inputs.
  • Write unit tests that push arithmetic to boundary values to ensure reverts.

screens.narratorSegment: This example demonstrates why older Solidity versions are dangerous for arithmetic. A transfer function that attempts to check the sender's balance using a subtraction in the require can actually underflow before the comparison, producing a very large result that passes the check. Concretely, if the sender's balance is less than the amount, balances[msg. sender] - amount underflows to a huge unsigned integer. The require therefore passes and the assignment balances[msg. sender] -= amount sets the sender's balance to another wrapped value, which can create effectively unlimited tokens for the attacker. This pattern was common before compiler-level checks. When reviewing legacy token contracts, look for expressions that perform arithmetic inside require conditions in a way that could underflow. Code Walkthrough › VulnerableToken (pre-0.8.0)

Underflow in transfer

Solidity example (vulnerable, older compiler)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.7.0; // older compiler example

contract VulnerableToken {
    mapping(address => uint256) public balances;
    uint256 public totalSupply;

    constructor(uint256 initialSupply) {
        totalSupply = initialSupply;
        balances[msg.sender] = initialSupply;
    }

    function transfer(address _to, uint256 _amount) public returns (bool) {
        require(balances[msg.sender] - _amount >= 0, "Insufficient balance"); // problematic

        balances[msg.sender] -= _amount; // underflow possible
        balances[_to] += _amount;
        return true;
    }
}
Why this fails
The subtraction inside require can underflow before the comparison in compilers without automatic checks. The underflow produces a large value and the require condition succeeds, leading to incorrect state changes.
Test tip

Write a unit test that calls transfer with amount greater than sender balance and assert the transaction reverts in secure code.

screens.title: Solidity 0.8.0+ and Secure Token
screens.narratorSegment: Solidity 0.8.0 introduced automatic overflow and underflow checks for arithmetic operations. That means operations like subtraction now revert when the result would go negative for unsigned integers. This simplifies secure coding: you can write straightforward arithmetic and rely on the compiler to prevent wrap-around. In the SecureToken example the subtraction balances[msg. sender] -= _amount will revert automatically if the sender lacks funds. Many teams still include explicit require checks for business clarity, but they are no longer necessary for safety. For older contracts that must remain on earlier compilers, SafeMath provides explicit checked functions. When migrating, update the pragma and re-run your full test suite to confirm arithmetic behavior. A useful test is to attempt a transfer with a larger amount than the balance and confirm the transaction reverts. Remember that compiler checks help, but you should still enforce clear invariants and reason about edge conditions like fee calculations or looped arithmetic that could overflow due to multiplication or exponent operations. Secure Example › SecureToken (0.8.0+)

Relying on built-in checks

Solidity example (safe with 0.8.0+)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0; // safe arithmetic by default

contract SecureToken {
    mapping(address => uint256) public balances;
    uint256 public totalSupply;

    constructor(uint256 initialSupply) {
        totalSupply = initialSupply;
        balances[msg.sender] = initialSupply;
    }

    function transfer(address _to, uint256 _amount) public returns (bool) {
        // subtraction will revert automatically if _amount > balances[msg.sender]
        balances[msg.sender] -= _amount;
        balances[_to] += _amount;
        return true;
    }
}

When upgrading to 0.8.0+, remove unsafe SafeMath uses and re-run tests. Keep explicit require checks if they clarify business rules.

Lab: implement vulnerable and secure vaults

Vulnerable contract (starter)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract EtherVaultVulnerable {
    mapping(address => uint256) public deposits;

    function deposit() public payable {
        deposits[msg.sender] += msg.value;
    }

    function withdraw(uint256 _amount) public {
        require(deposits[msg.sender] >= _amount, "Insufficient funds");

        // TODO: make an external call here BEFORE updating state to create the vulnerability

        // deposits[msg.sender] -= _amount; // update state AFTER external call to be vulnerable
    }

    function getContractBalance() public view returns (uint256) {
        return address(this).balance;
    }
}
Lab steps & test plan
  1. Complete withdraw to call msg.sender.call{{value:_amount}} before decrementing deposits.
  2. Write an attacker contract with a fallback that calls withdraw when receiving Ether.
  3. Write Hardhat tests that assert the vulnerable vault is drained and the secure vault resists the exploit.

screens.title: Testing and Defensive Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Writing tests that reproduce attacker behavior is the most reliable way to validate your defenses. For reentrancy, deploy both the victim and an attacker contract in a local Hardhat environment. Have the attacker deposit into the victim and then call the vulnerable withdraw to trigger its fallback and attempt reentry. Assert that the vulnerable contract's balance falls and that the secure contract resists the same sequence. For arithmetic, write tests that push values to boundary conditions: attempt transfers or calculations that would overflow or underflow and assert that a revert occurs on secure code. Don't assume gas stipends or EVM subtlety protect you; tests should use realistic gas and attacker logic. Additional defensive patterns include minimizing the logic executed during external calls, preferring pull patterns for payments, adding events to audit sensitive operations, and documenting invariants clearly in code. A common mistake is relying only on manual code reviews without tests—automated tests that simulate attacks catch regressions and protect your contract through future refactors. Make these tests part of your CI pipeline. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn two classes of vulnerabilities that have repeatedly caused large losses in smart contracts: reentrancy and integer over/underflows. We'll build a mental model for how external calls can be abused to re-enter a function before state updates happen, and how low-level integer arithmetic can silently wrap values in older Solidity versions. You will see concrete vulnerable examples, step through an exploit pattern, and learn practical mitigations you can apply immediately: the Checks-Effects-Interactions ordering, using reentrancy guards, and relying on Solidity 0.8.0's built-in arithmetic checks or SafeMath for legacy code. Knowing these patterns matters because defenses are simple to apply but, when omitted, they enable trivial automatic drains and token minting bugs. As you follow the examples, think of each rule as a small discipline: update state before sending funds, lock critical functions while executing, and prefer compiler-level checks for arithmetic. By the end you'll be able to identify risky code, fix it, and design tests that simulate real attacker behavior.

This first set of objectives focuses on reentrancy and immediate defenses. First, you'll be able to identify a reentrancy vulnerability by recognizing external calls that happen before state updates and the classic withdrawal pattern that allows callbacks. You'll also learn to implement the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern so that state is adjusted before any external calls happen, preventing reentry-based drains. Third, you'll adopt a reentrancy guard pattern or mutex to lock functions during execution, which is a complementary protection in more complex flows. Finally, you'll practice analyzing real-world exploit scenarios to see how simple ordering mistakes become catastrophic when combined with attacker contracts. Each objective emphasizes not only what to change in code but why that change prevents the exploit. For example, updating balances before sending Ether removes the attacker's ability to withdraw repeatedly because the invariant that the contract relies on has already been modified. These skills are practical: you'll use them when reviewing withdrawals, escrow flows, or any function that interacts with external addresses.

This second group of objectives covers integer safety and testing. You will recognize integer overflow and underflow conditions in contracts that use fixed-size unsigned integers, and understand how value wrapping can produce absurd balances or negative-like results. You will learn to prefer Solidity 0.8.0 or later because these compilers revert arithmetic operations that would overflow or underflow, removing an entire class of bugs. For legacy code or specific control needs, you'll learn when to use SafeMath-style checked arithmetic and how it enforces explicit checks before performing operations. Finally, you will practice applying these mitigations in token transfers and supply logic, and you will design tests that assert arithmetic reverts when given out-of-range inputs. This matters because the correctness of token accounting and balances is foundational: a single unchecked subtraction can result in effectively minting tokens or emptying accounts, undermining trust and causing financial loss.

Reentrancy is a class of vulnerability that happens when a contract makes an external call and the callee is able to call back into the original contract before the original function has finished updating its internal state. The key problem is timing: the contract assumes that once it calls out, the rest of the function runs in isolation, but an attacker can break that assumption by implementing a fallback or receive function that calls back. A helpful analogy is a vending machine that dispenses a soda before updating its inventory. If you can repeatedly trigger the dispenser before the inventory count is decremented, you can get more sodas than you paid for. In Solidity, calls such as low-level call with value or transfer can invoke code on the recipient. If the recipient is a malicious contract with a callback that re-enters the withdraw function, it can withdraw multiple times while the balance still indicates available funds. Concrete example: a withdrawal function that sends Ether and then decrements the user's balance is vulnerable because the decrement hasn't happened when the external call executes. A common misconception is that the Ethereum transaction model serializes everything and prevents reentry; it does not. Transactions are atomic at the EVM level, but external calls execute user-defined code which can call back into any public or external function on the original contract during the same transaction. The core takeaway is to never rely on state that will be changed after an external call. Instead, order your operations so the contract's internal invariants are preserved before making external calls.

Let's walk through a short vulnerable withdrawal contract so you can see exactly what to look for in code. The core pattern is: check balance, send Ether via a call, then update the balance. The problem is that the external call gives control to the recipient before the balance is decremented. In our vulnerable example the function uses a low-level call to send Ether and only after confirming success does it subtract from the sender's balance. An attacker implements a fallback that calls withdraw again. Because the balance has not changed, the second call passes the require and sends Ether again. This repeats until the contract's Ether is drained or gas runs out. When you read real code, watch for any use of msg. sender. call{value:...} or transfer followed by state changes. Even if transfer imposes a gas stipend, complex interactions or proxy patterns can still present windows for reentry. The correct fix will reorder the operations and optionally add a reentrancy guard. As you study this snippet, imagine an attacker contract that calls withdraw from its fallback. That mental model helps you write tests that mimic the exploit.

Understanding the exploit sequence helps you design tests and mitigations. The attack begins when the attacker deposits funds into the victim contract or otherwise gains a valid balance. Next the attacker calls the vulnerable withdraw function. The function performs the require check and then immediately performs an external call to send Ether. At that moment control passes to the attacker contract, which implements a fallback or receive handler that calls withdraw again. Because the original function has not yet decremented the attacker's balance, the check still passes and another external transfer occurs. The attacker repeats this call sequence until the victim contract's balance is drained. Tests that demonstrate this pattern should include an attacker contract that calls back during the external call and assertions that the victim's balance decreases while the attacker's internal accounting grows incorrectly. A common mitigation step is to reorder steps so state is updated before the external call, breaking the exploit sequence. Locks, such as a reentrancy guard, also interrupt the repeated calls by preventing the second call from entering the same function while it is already running. Thinking in sequences teaches you to close each reentry window.

The Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern is the simplest and most widely recommended defense against reentrancy. It prescribes ordering: first perform all checks, then make state changes, and only finally interact with external contracts. This ensures that if an external call attempts to reenter, the necessary state invariants have already been updated and the reentry fails or has no effect. In practice this means moving balance decrements ahead of Ether transfers or external calls. Another common refinement is to use a withdraw-pull pattern: let users request a balance and then pull funds themselves rather than the contract pushing funds automatically. The corrected SecureWithdrawal example demonstrates this: the require check is done, the balance is decremented, and then the external call is executed. Also consider adding a reentrancy guard as an additional safety net. When you refactor code, run the same exploit tests against the new contract. A correctly refactored contract will not allow the attacker fallback to withdraw again because the balance no longer permits it. Remember that ordering and invariants are your first line of defense. Checks-Effects-Interactions in Practice means checks first, update state second, call external addresses last to close reentrancy windows.. In practical terms, refactor the vulnerable function to prevent reentrancy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A reentrancy guard is a simple pattern that uses a state variable as a mutex to prevent a function from being entered while it is already executing. OpenZeppelin's ReentrancyGuard is a common implementation: it sets a status flag when entering a protected function and clears it on exit. If a reentrant call tries to enter while the flag is set, the guard reverts. This approach is particularly useful when complex state updates or multiple external calls make a pure ordering solution difficult. However, guards should be used thoughtfully: they add a global lock for the function, which can change contract behavior in legitimate nested scenarios. In practice, combine a guard with Checks-Effects-Interactions for robust protection. A common misconception is that a guard alone is always sufficient; it is a strong safety net, but correct ordering and minimal external calls are still best practices. When writing tests, protect a function with a guard and confirm that an attacker fallback causes a revert instead of permitting repeated withdrawals. The guard provides clarity: if any nested call attempts to re-enter, the contract explicitly denies it.

When sending Ether from a contract you will commonly see three mechanisms: transfer, send, and call with value. Historically transfer forwarded a fixed, small gas stipend and was considered safer against reentrancy because it limited what the recipient could do in its fallback. However, that gas stipend is often insufficient for modern recipient contracts and can cause failures. The low-level call with value is now the most common pattern because it forwards all available gas, which is necessary for interacting with complex recipient logic, but it also creates a larger reentrancy surface because the callee has more gas to run arbitrary code including callbacks. The key point is that the choice of call mechanism is orthogonal to the ordering rule: even a transfer can be problematic if the contract relies on state updates happening later. Thus you should write code assuming any external call may execute complicated logic. Prefer call with value when you need it, but always update critical state and, where appropriate, combine this with a reentrancy guard. Tests should exercise calls with realistic gas assumptions to ensure an attacker can or cannot perform reentry as expected. Don't rely on gas limits as your primary defense.

Integer overflow happens when an arithmetic operation produces a value larger than the type can represent and the value wraps around to the minimum. Integer underflow is the opposite: an operation results in a value below the minimum and wraps to the maximum. In unsigned integers used throughout Solidity, underflow often wraps to a very large number. For example, on an 8-bit unsigned integer, incrementing 255 yields 0; decrementing 0 yields 255. In token accounting this wrap-around can lead to effectively minting large balances or zeroing out supply checks. Before Solidity 0.8.0 these operations did not revert automatically, and developers relied on libraries like SafeMath to explicitly check for dangerous conditions before performing arithmetic. A common misconception is assuming that require checks like balances[msg. sender] - amount >= 0 will protect you; in older solc versions subtraction underflow happens prior to the comparison, which invalidates the guard. The practical advice is to use Solidity 0.8.0 or later to get built-in checks, and in legacy code adopt SafeMath or equivalent checks. Always include tests that attempt out-of-range arithmetic to ensure your contract reverts instead of silently wrapping.

This example demonstrates why older Solidity versions are dangerous for arithmetic. A transfer function that attempts to check the sender's balance using a subtraction in the require can actually underflow before the comparison, producing a very large result that passes the check. Concretely, if the sender's balance is less than the amount, balances[msg. sender] - amount underflows to a huge unsigned integer. The require therefore passes and the assignment balances[msg. sender] -= amount sets the sender's balance to another wrapped value, which can create effectively unlimited tokens for the attacker. This pattern was common before compiler-level checks. When reviewing legacy token contracts, look for expressions that perform arithmetic inside require conditions in a way that could underflow. The safe migration is to move to Solidity 0.8.0+ where subtraction reverts on underflow, or to use SafeMath functions like sub() that explicitly check bounds. Tests should simulate transfers with amounts greater than the balance and assert that the transaction reverts rather than altering balances unexpectedly. Solidity 0.8.0 introduced automatic overflow and underflow checks for arithmetic operations. That means operations like subtraction now revert when the result would go negative for unsigned integers. This simplifies secure coding: you can write straightforward arithmetic and rely on the compiler to prevent wrap-around. In the SecureToken example the subtraction balances[msg. sender] -= _amount will revert automatically if the sender lacks funds. Many teams still include explicit require checks for business clarity, but they are no longer necessary for safety. For older contracts that must remain on earlier compilers, SafeMath provides explicit checked functions. When migrating, update the pragma and re-run your full test suite to confirm arithmetic behavior. A useful test is to attempt a transfer with a larger amount than the balance and confirm the transaction reverts. Remember that compiler checks help, but you should still enforce clear invariants and reason about edge conditions like fee calculations or looped arithmetic that could overflow due to multiplication or exponent operations. This lab asks you to implement two contracts and a test harness. First, complete EtherVaultVulnerable's withdraw function so it performs the external call before updating state. Deploy that contract and write a malicious attacker contract with a fallback that calls withdraw again. In your Hardhat test, send deposits into the vulnerable vault, execute the attacker exploit, and assert that the vault's balance is drained. Next, implement EtherVaultSecure following the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern: require check, state decrement, then external call. Re-deploy the secure vault and run the same attacker test; it should fail to drain funds. The task teaches both diagnosis and mitigation: you will see how a minimal order change blocks the exploit. A common testing pitfall is not simulating realistic gas behavior—configure your test environment to allow the attacker fallback to run meaningful logic. Finally, document the failing and succeeding assertions in your tests so you can reproduce the difference when running continuous checks. Writing tests that reproduce attacker behavior is the most reliable way to validate your defenses. For reentrancy, deploy both the victim and an attacker contract in a local Hardhat environment. Have the attacker deposit into the victim and then call the vulnerable withdraw to trigger its fallback and attempt reentry. Assert that the vulnerable contract's balance falls and that the secure contract resists the same sequence. For arithmetic, write tests that push values to boundary conditions: attempt transfers or calculations that would overflow or underflow and assert that a revert occurs on secure code. Don't assume gas stipends or EVM subtlety protect you; tests should use realistic gas and attacker logic. Additional defensive patterns include minimizing the logic executed during external calls, preferring pull patterns for payments, adding events to audit sensitive operations, and documenting invariants clearly in code. A common mistake is relying only on manual code reviews without tests—automated tests that simulate attacks catch regressions and protect your contract through future refactors. Make these tests part of your CI pipeline. Let's summarize the essential ideas you should carry forward. First, reentrancy happens when an external call allows the callee to call back into the contract before state updates finish; ordering state changes before calls prevents many attacks. Second, the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern—validate inputs, update state, then make external calls—is the canonical rule to follow. Third, a reentrancy guard provides a useful mutex that reverts nested calls and is a valuable complementary defense. Each of these reduces the window in which an attacker can manipulate contract execution. Keep these simple practices in your coding checklist and apply them to any function that transfers funds or calls unknown contracts. A second quick summary focuses on integer safety and practical development steps. Understand that integer overflow and underflow allow values to wrap and corrupt accounting in older Solidity compilers. Prefer Solidity 0.8.0 and later because arithmetic now reverts on out-of-range operations. For legacy code, use SafeMath-style checked arithmetic functions. Always write boundary tests that push arithmetic to extremes and assert reverts, and include exploit tests that emulate an attacker.
